source.title: [Interim research report] Taking features out of superposition with sparse autoencoders

record.file_problem: none; the full post, appendix, and comments are present
record.tranche_reason: The study tests sparse-autoencoder feature recovery on synthetic data with known generating features, then applies indirect recovery diagnostics to a small language model. It does not reproduce the original toy-network superposition experiments.
record.gate_note: The synthetic-data recovery results do not test whether a network learns superposition, and the study has no ground truth features for its language-model experiments. Dead-neuron counts and reconstruction/L1 loss plots are used as hyperparameter-selection diagnostics, so they are not recorded as feature-recovery outcome rows. Values visible only in plots are not assigned exact numbers unless the text describes them.
record.test_reason: The language-model part fits SAEs to a 31M-parameter transformer's MLP activations. It checks whether consistent sparse features are recovered, which bears on V4 and V5. The toy-data part fits SAEs to hand-generated synthetic data and trains no network, so it does not test V1–V3.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that a simple L1 SAE recovers ground-truth features in toy data. The language-model diagnostics differ from the toy results and are inconclusive. They add very weak, tentative evidence of more than 100k features in a 256-dimensional model, which would make the method costly to scale. In a later comment the author says the language-model SAEs were probably undertrained.
record.recipe_differences: The study generates sparse synthetic activations from known feature directions and fits an L1-regularized autoencoder, then applies the method to a small transformer's MLP activations. It does not train toy networks and measure their superposition geometry as in the original source.
record.method_sensitivity: Feature-recovery diagnostics vary with L1 penalty and dictionary size; the authors report an interaction between these choices. The language-model dictionary comparisons remain inconclusive across the tested settings.

fits_no_version.finding: On synthetic data built from sparse combinations of 512 random directions in 256 dimensions, an L1 SAE recovers the generating directions. This holds for L1 values of ~0.03–0.3 and dictionaries 1–8× the ground-truth size, with an L1 × size interaction. Denoising SAEs are slightly worse.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sparse autoencoders can recover known generating directions from synthetic sparse superposed data, with recovery depending on the L1 penalty and dictionary size.

record.problems: The authors call the report preliminary and incomplete. The language-model results have no ground-truth features, dictionary comparisons provide only indirect evidence, and the authors raise possible undertraining, insufficient data, noise, and mismatches between synthetic and model activations. The main-text language-model plots focus on one layer; exact MMCS values and formal uncertainty estimates are not given.
record.rows_left_out: Dead-neuron counts and reconstruction/L1 loss plots (Figures 4–9 and 11–12) are used as hyperparameter diagnostics rather than direct feature-recovery outcomes. Other language-model layers appear in appendix plots, but the text does not describe separate layer-specific results.

untested.parts: No toy network is trained. Superposition is hand-constructed with random directions at G=2h, so learned geometry and sparsity transitions are not measured.
Feature importance and capacity competition are not examined.
Other causes of polysemanticity are not examined.
Completeness, canonicality and stability across seeds at fixed size are not measured. Only cross-size similarity is reported.
Not tested. The authors only speculate that a feature might be a distribution over directions.
Only one small model is tested, and layer-specific outcomes beyond layer 1 are not described in the text. There is no interpretability analysis of the features.

missing.what: Language-model dead-neuron result: no dead neurons appear even at 102400 features. The authors read this as very weak, tentative evidence of over 100k features in superposition for d_model=256. This bears on V4 and was excluded as a hyperparameter diagnostic.
missing.locator: Identifying the overcomplete feature basis, 'Dead neurons', Figure 11; Conclusion

missing.what: Language-model SSLL loss-stickiness result: no clear peaks and a flat region near 32381 features, too different from the toy data to estimate dictionary size.

record.verdict_notes: The toy setting uses hand-sampled feature directions, not a trained network, so V1 is not tested. The V4 and V5 verdicts are weak because the authors themselves call the language-model results preliminary and possibly due to undertraining. The L1 term was divided by dictionary size, which the author later called a mistake that complicated hyperparameter search.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not train toy networks to represent more features than dimensions or measure their learned superposition geometry.
It does not test whether feature importance or capacity competition causes some features to receive dedicated dimensions and others to share.
It does not test other causes of polysemantic neurons.

The language-model experiments lack ground-truth features, so they cannot establish whether the SAE recovered the model's actual sparse features. The study examines only a small model and reports results for layer 1 in the main text.

The study compares dictionaries of different sizes as an indirect consistency diagnostic, but does not establish feature completeness, canonicality, or stability across repeated runs under the same conditions.
It does not test whether features in a network are inherently one-dimensional rather than multidimensional.

rows.subject: toy data (h=256, G=512)
rows.operation_detail: Measured mean max cosine similarity (MMCS) between SAE dictionary features and known generating features across L1 penalties.
rows.value: High MMCS across an acceptable L1 range of approximately 0.03 to 0.3; no exact MMCS value stated.
rows.note: The authors describe this as a range in which the autoencoder recovers the ground-truth features.

rows.subject: toy data (h=256, G=512)
rows.operation_detail: Measured MMCS between learned dictionary features and known generating features across dictionary sizes.
rows.baseline: dictionary size equal to the ground-truth feature count is described as optimal
rows.value: The authors report almost complete recovery for dictionary sizes 1–8× the ground-truth size, with MMCS decreasing slowly as size increases; exact values not stated.

rows.subject: toy data (h=256, G=512)
rows.operation_detail: Measured MMCS while jointly varying dictionary size and L1 penalty.
rows.value: Larger dictionaries require larger L1 penalties for high feature recovery; no exact values stated.
rows.note: The authors describe an interaction between dictionary size and the optimal L1 penalty.

rows.subject: toy data (h=256, G=512)
rows.operation_detail: Measured MMCS for sparse denoising autoencoders against known generating features.
rows.value: Denoising autoencoders recover the ground-truth features; MMCS is usually very slightly worse than for the noiseless L1 counterpart. The text reports little interaction between L1 coefficient and noise standard deviation.
rows.note: The post does not state exact MMCS values.

rows.subject: small six-layer transformer (31 million parameters)
rows.stage_stated: trained by the authors on the Wikipedia subset of the Pile dataset
rows.operation_detail: Compared MMCS between SAE dictionaries of different sizes as an indirect diagnostic of feature recovery and dictionary consistency.
rows.measure: MMCS between dictionaries of different sizes
rows.value: MMCS between dictionaries never exceeds approximately 0.4; the text says features learned in dictionaries of different sizes are often quite different.
rows.locator: “Mean max cosine similarity between a dictionary and those larger than it,” Figure 13 and text
rows.note: This is an indirect proxy only: the authors say they cannot draw firm conclusions about optimal dictionary size or ground-truth recovery from these plots. Other layers appear in appendix plots, but the text does not describe their specific outcomes.
rows.check: The link and state are acceptable. It is an indirect proxy with no ground truth: MMCS between dictionaries of different sizes is ≤~0.4, against high values on toy data. For V4 it shows recovery was not established rather than absent. For V5 it shows features vary with dictionary size.

source_check.correct: V4: cannot_determine; cross-dictionary similarity does not establish whether ground-truth sparse features were recovered. V5: partial is appropriate for the observed dependence on dictionary size.
source_check.locator_found: Methods: Small transformer trained on natural language data; language-model results, Figure 13 and preceding paragraph, lines 154–157.
source_check.problem: The shared partial state conflates demonstrated dictionary inconsistency with inconclusive evidence about V4 feature recovery.

relationships.condition: 31M-parameter transformer, MLP layer 1, SAEs up to 102400 features
relationships.reason: Cross-size dictionary MMCS stayed ≤~0.4 (r5). Loss and dead-neuron diagnostics did not match the toy data, so recovery of sparse features was not established. The authors give only very weak evidence of >100k features and attribute the mismatch partly to undertraining or noise.
relationships.display_finding: Dictionaries of different sizes agreed only weakly (MMCS at most about 0.4), and loss and dead-neuron diagnostics did not match the toy data, which the authors partly attribute to undertraining or noise. They give only very weak evidence of more than 100k features.

source_check.notes: The author's retrospective strongly suspects undertraining and regrets publishing a specific feature-count estimate. The tentative count is not an established lower bound.

statements.correction: 31M-parameter, six-layer transformer; second MLP layer; cross-size dictionary MMCS never exceeds approximately 0.4; ground-truth feature recovery remains undetermined; dictionary-size dependence bears on V5 stability.
statements.problem: The facts about this study are accurate, but inconclusive recovery diagnostics do not establish a scope limitation on V4.
